# Environmental exposure as a demand driver

Research published in *The Lancet Planetary Health* estimates that long-term
exposure to air pollution is associated with roughly **1.5 million additional
deaths per year in India** relative to a counterfactual in which the country met
WHO exposure guidelines. Analyses of PM2.5-attributable mortality attribute
approximately **half of that burden to cardiovascular effects**, and in
studies of major Indian cities **ischaemic heart disease accounts for around 47
per cent** of PM2.5-attributable deaths.

Dose-response work reports increases in cardiovascular mortality for every
10 µg/m³ increment in PM2.5, with effect sizes varying widely by study design.

## Why this matters for prioritisation

The case explicitly asks about "environmental shifts (e.g. air quality,
climate-linked disease incidence)". The mechanism is real and well evidenced,
and it pushes incidence of ischaemic events - which is the demand driver behind
anti-anginal therapy and secondary-prevention lipid combinations.

This signal is deliberately given a **small magnitude and medium confidence**.
The epidemiological link is strong, but the translation from ambient PM2.5 to
incremental prescriptions in a specific molecule class over five years is
indirect. It should nudge the view, not drive it. Any recommendation that
depends materially on this signal alone should be treated as speculative.
